analysis.one_liner: Mandates an offshore oil and gas lease sale off Virginia and splits the royalties between the state, cleanup, and energy programs.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in committee when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require the Interior Department to hold a proposed offshore oil and gas lease sale (Lease Sale 220) in federal waters at least 50 miles off Virginia's coast within a year of a request from Virginia's governor. Half the money from the leases would go to non-federal uses: 75 percent of that share to Virginia (for schools, transportation, tax cuts, or energy projects), with smaller shares for land conservation and an environmental damage cleanup fund. The other half would go to the federal government, split between paying down the debt and a new Alternative Energy Trust Fund funding coal technologies, forest biomass, solar, wind, renewable energy, methane hydrate research, nuclear loan guarantees, and smart grid work. No drilling could occur within 50 miles of the coast unless the governor asked, and tracts that the Defense Department said would conflict with military operations would be off-limits.
analysis.who_benefits: Virginians would gain a dedicated stream of lease revenue for state priorities like education and transportation, and the oil and gas industry would gain access to new federal drilling leases off the Atlantic coast. Alternative energy sectors — including coal technology, nuclear, solar, and wind — would gain a new grant fund.

how_it_helps.text: Directs the Interior Secretary to hold Lease Sale 220 offshore Virginia within one year of a governor's petition, rather than leaving the timing to the department's own scheduling.

Sends 75 percent of the non-federal half of lease revenues directly to Virginia without a further appropriation, usable for education, transportation, tax reduction, coastal restoration, energy infrastructure, and disaster insurance programs.

Sets aside 12.5 percent of the non-federal half for environmental mitigation of any drilling damage, including damage not caused by negligence, and requires federal half revenues to be split between debt reduction and an Alternative Energy Trust Fund for coal technologies, biomass, solar, wind, renewables, methane hydrate research, nuclear loan guarantees, and smart grid projects.
Bars leasing within 50 miles of Virginia's coastal zone unless the governor requests it and excludes any tract the Defense Department says would interfere with military operations.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury gives up most lease revenue that would otherwise flow to the government. Coastal communities, fisheries, and tourism businesses bear the risk of oil spills in the Atlantic, which the bill acknowledges by pre-funding a mitigation account for damage 'regardless of whether' it is foreseeable or caused by negligence or a natural disaster.

drawbacks.text: The bill itself anticipates spill damage by requiring a dedicated account to mitigate 'any environmental damage that occurs as a result of extraction activities... regardless of whether the damage is reasonably foreseeable' or caused by negligence or a natural disaster, an implicit acknowledgment that offshore drilling off Virginia carries environmental risk to the coast, fisheries, and tourism.

Mandating the lease sale on a one-year clock removes the Interior Department's discretion over whether, when, and on what terms public offshore resources are offered for drilling, and most lease royalties would no longer flow to the federal government.
The bill would expand fossil fuel extraction in the Atlantic, with the environmental and climate costs that entails, as the price for the state revenue and alternative energy fund it creates.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The revenue split is generous to the public side by offshore-drilling standards — most money goes to Virginia, land conservation, cleanup, debt reduction, and energy research rather than being kept general. But the bill's core trade is real: a guaranteed new stream of state money in exchange for industrial drilling off the Virginia coast, with the spill risk borne by coastal communities and the mandate written so the sale happens on a clock once the governor asks.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and then two subcommittees, but no committee ever held a hearing or vote on it, and it expired when the 111th Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Representative Bob Goodlatte introduced the bill on March 25, 2010, joined as original sponsors by six other members of the Virginia delegation — Republicans Wolf, Wittman, Cantor, and Forbes and Democrats Nye, Boucher, and Perriello.

It was referred to the Natural Resources, Energy and Commerce, and Science and Technology Committees, and then to subcommittees on Energy and Mineral Resources and Energy and Environment in early April 2010.
No further action was ever recorded; the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote, and died when the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The status quo held: no Atlantic lease sale was mandated, so coastal and fishing interests avoided new drilling risk, while Virginia got no new revenue stream and the oil and gas industry missed a chance at new leases. With a bill this stalled, no side gained much.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo held; no one gained much

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan — seven cosponsors split 4 Republicans and 3 Democrats, and all eight original sponsors were Virginians from both parties — but no vote was ever taken, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: The bill would hand the industry new lease access to federal Atlantic waters off Virginia, with a mandatory one-year sale clock once the governor petitions. The public shares in royalties and gets a 50-mile coastal buffer and a pre-funded spill mitigation account, but bears the environmental risk of drilling.
A coal and related technologies grant program would be funded from the new Alternative Energy Trust Fund, a direct subsidy stream for coal-region interests.
The trust fund could be used for nuclear power loan guarantees, federal backing that lowers financing costs for new plants.

industries.industry: Renewable energy (solar, wind, biomass, smart grid)
industries.note: Grants for solar, wind, renewable energy, forest biomass, methane hydrate research, and smart grid technology would come from the trust fund, though the amounts depend entirely on drilling royalties materializing.

industries.industry: Virginia state government and coastal tourism/fishing interests
industries.note: The state would receive a guaranteed 37.5 percent of lease revenue for education, transportation, and other uses, while coastal tourism and fishing businesses face the downside risk of drilling damage, for which the bill sets aside a 6.25 percent mitigation share.
